Definition: Whether the country has an operational Internet Exchange Point (IXP) and its maturity. IXPs enable local internet traffic to be exchanged domestically rather than being routed internationally, reducing latency, costs, and dependence on foreign infrastructure. Critical for local digital ecosystem development.
Comments: Nigeria has active IXP presence via IXPN (Nigeria Internet Exchange Point) with operational exchanges (e.g., Lagos, Abuja) indicating active IXPs with participation.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Upgraded from 4 to 5. IXPN now operates 13 exchange points nationwide (Lagos, Abuja, Port Harcourt, Enugu, Kano, Delta, Gombe), has 130+ members including Google, Meta, Microsoft, TikTok, Amazon and all Nigerian MNOs, is MANRS-compliant, and carried 1.7 Tbps of peak traffic by early 2026 (up from 1 Tbps in April 2025) — evidencing a mature, broadly-participated IXP ecosystem rather than merely 'moderate participation'.

Definition: Unique mobile subscriber penetration rate as a percentage of the total population. Measures the proportion of individuals who subscribe to a mobile service (not SIM cards, which can be multiple per person). Mobile phones are the primary device for internet access in Africa.
Comments: ITU country profile reports mobile-cellular subscriptions per 100 inhabitants = 102 (2022), implying high penetration (55–69%+ unique likely; using subscriptions as proxy gives score 4).
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW. The original score relied on mobile-cellular subscriptions per 100 (102, ITU 2022) — a SIM/connections measure, not the unique-subscriber penetration the variable requires; Nigeria has high multi-SIM ownership so this proxy is not appropriate. GSMA's own country data put unique-subscriber penetration at ~49-52% in 2018, trending towards 55% by 2025, and 2024 NCC data show a sharp fall in active subscriptions (224.7m to 164.9m) following NIN-SIM deduplication, making the true current unique-subscriber % genuinely unclear from freely available sources (GSMA Intelligence's precise current figure is paywalled). This sits close to the 40-54%/55-69% band boundary — flagged for human review rather than guessed.

Definition: The availability and presence of major cloud service providers (hyperscale and regional) operating in or serving the country with local or near-local infrastructure. Cloud availability determines access to scalable computing resources for government, business, and startups.
Value Name: Regional cloud availability zone nearby (same sub-region)
Comments: Major hyperscalers lack full Nigeria regions; reporting indicates AWS launched a Local Zone in Lagos (2023) but no full-scale hyperscale region, implying regional/limited local presence.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Upgraded from 3 to 4. AWS operates a Local Zone in Lagos (since 2023) with expanded Direct Connect capacity (100G, Sept 2025), giving Nigeria a genuine local hyperscale presence/edge node rather than only remote regional service from Cape Town/Johannesburg; MTN's Dabengwa Data Centre (Lagos, Tier III, 4.5MW) also offers local commercial IaaS. No full AWS/Azure/GCP 'region' exists in-country, so this stops short of band 5.

Definition: Whether the country has enacted legal or regulatory requirements mandating that certain categories of data (personal data, government data, financial data, or critical infrastructure data) be stored within national borders. Central to data sovereignty debates in Africa.
Value Name: Sectoral requirements only (e.g., financial or telecoms data)
Comments: Nigeria has sectoral localisation rules (e.g., NITDA ICT Guidelines require telecom/network service companies host subscriber data in Nigeria; government 'sovereign data' to be hosted locally), indicating sectoral/localisation requirements rather than universal.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed as sectoral. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 (ss.41-43) and the 2025 General Application and Implementation Directive regulate cross-border transfer via adequacy/consent rather than blanket localisation; a NITDA data-classification framework proposing mandatory in-country storage of sensitive finance/health/government data remains unpublished/draft as of September 2025. This still matches 'sectoral requirements only', now evidenced with the primary Act text and NDPC guidance rather than a single 2021 secondary PDF.

Definition: Whether the government has established dedicated data center infrastructure and/or a government cloud (G-Cloud) strategy for hosting e-government services and public sector data domestically. Critical for data sovereignty and e-government service delivery.
Value Name: National data center operational with cloud strategy adopted
Comments: Nigeria adopted a National Cloud Computing Policy (Aug 2019) with a 'Cloud First' thrust for government institutions, indicating operational strategy framework.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed and refreshed. Galaxy Backbone's National Shared Services Data Centre (Abuja, Tier III/IV-certified, with a secondary facility in Enugu) has long served as the Federal Government's national data centre, and NITDA's National Cloud Policy 2025 (superseding the 2019 policy cited originally) formalises a mandatory 'Cloud First' directive, a Sovereign Cloud Governance Committee and a government Digital Marketplace. This still matches 'national data centre operational with cloud strategy adopted'; evidence of full active migration needed for band 5 is not yet established.

Comments: ESMAP presentation notes Rural Electrification Agency developed Off-Grid Electrification Strategy and NERC mini-grid regulations (2016) supporting deployment, indicating active policy with some deployment.
redteam_note: Only one source for a substantive score — corroborate.
revision_notes: Confirmed. The Rural Electrification Agency's Nigeria Electrification Project continues active deployment via Performance-Based Grants and Minimum Subsidy Tenders (targeting 1,100+ mini-grids), underpinned by the Electricity Act 2023 and the World Bank-backed DARES programme; by 2023 reporting, 138,000 homes had been connected via 16 completed mini-grids. This is a materially more current and detailed evidence base than the 2017 ESMAP presentation cited originally, but deployment remains partial relative to national need, so 'active policy with some deployment' still fits better than a 'comprehensive... significant deployment' score.
